title: Maidenhead Grid Locator: Ham Radio Squares
description: Convert between coordinates and Maidenhead locator squares with the Maidenhead Grid Locator — the amateur radio grid, field to subsquare. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Times Square sits in locator FN30as, and London in IO91wm — six characters that ham operators exchange instead of addresses, precise to about 5 × 4 km.
quick_answer: The Maidenhead Grid Locator converts between latitude/longitude and Maidenhead locator squares — the hierarchical grid amateur radio uses to exchange locations. Enter a point and read its locator, from the 2-letter field down to the 6-character subsquare, or reverse a locator to the square it names.
steps_intro: The grid the world's radio amateurs navigate by:

body.t: Contests and awards (VUCC, grid chasing) run on locators. Know yours before the pileup asks — and the station you worked gets logged by square, not by town.
On the high bands, contacts are grid-to-grid achievements. The locator frames what 'far' means when the band opens.
QRZ pages and logs speak locators. The converter translates them into the geography the rest of this site uses.
Rare squares are destinations ('gridpeditions'). Find which square a summit or island activates before the drive.
FN is the field (20° × 10°), 30 the square (2° × 1°), 'as' the subsquare (~5.0 × 4.2 km at that latitude). Each pair refines by ten or twenty-four — the hierarchy in one string.
The world's most exchanged locator family starts IO91 — the square containing London. Operators who have never visited can place it instantly, which is the system's entire magic.

popular_table.note: Adopted in Maidenhead, England in 1980 by VHF managers — hence the name. The system covers the globe in 32,400 fields' tidy hierarchy.

faq: What does this tool calculate?
The Maidenhead locator for a coordinate pair (to subsquare or extended precision), and the square's location for a locator — the standard IARU system.
Do I need an account?
No — coordinates or locator in, answer out; no callsign required either.
Can I use the result for professional work?
For amateur radio, awards and planning it is the standard itself. Professional surveying uses other frames, as everywhere.
Which datum do these coordinate tools use?
WGS84 — the frame GPS produces and web maps consume.
Do more decimal places always mean better accuracy?
No — resolution is not accuracy; the precision tools on this site price each decimal place in metres.
Can I copy the result into GIS software?
Locators paste as labels; the square's corner coordinates convert onward into GIS via the bounding tools.
Case matters?
Convention: field and subsquare letters as given (fields uppercase, subsquares usually lowercase) — parsers are case-tolerant, humans are traditionalists.
Ocean squares?
Every point on Earth has a locator, sea included — maritime mobiles exchange them like everyone else.
My square straddles a border.
Most do — the grid ignores politics completely, which operators consider a feature.
Extended precision beyond 6 characters?
The 8-character extended square (~700 × 500 m) serves microwave work; the hierarchy continues by the same alternating pattern.
Antipodes?
Every square has one; DXers plan around the antipode's greyline like sailors around weather.
